title: Resampling Amplification: When Defer-to-Resample Helps the Attacker

original_idea.body:
# Resampling Amplification: When Defer-to-Resample Helps the Attacker

**Problem:** Risk: a control protocol meant to improve safety actively reduces it. Causal chain: monitor flags a suspicious action -> protocol resamples the untrusted model for fresh candidates -> lowest-suspicion sample is taken -> if the input contains an injection, resampling re-rolls the same attack until it lands. Recent work found Defer-to-Resample can BACKFIRE, dropping safety to 17% under adaptive attacks. The under-studied link is which input characteristics make resampling amplify rather than dilute an attack.

**Direction:** Build a tiny resampling harness: for a set of agent inputs (some containing injected instructions), sample N candidate actions from an open model and apply defer-to-resample logic with a monitor. Vary injection strength and measure attack success vs. N. Identify the regime where more resampling = more attack success (amplification) vs. dilution.

**Why it matters:** Resampling is a celebrated recent control technique; the discovery that it can backfire is exactly the kind of surprising result worth replicating and mapping. Characterizing the amplification regime tells blue teams when NOT to resample. Small-scale, open-model, no lab infra.

**Relevant context:** Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling (arXiv:2504.10374) introduces resample protocols exploiting model statelessness; reports safety gains 50%->96%. Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors (arXiv:2510.09462) shows Defer-to-Resample amplifies prompt injection, dropping safety to 17% under adaptive evaluation.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused first deliverable (amplification-vs-dilution regime curve) with few dependencies.

title: Schelling-Signal Discovery Rate Between Untrusted Policy and Untrusted Monitor

original_idea.body:
# Schelling-Signal Discovery Rate Between Untrusted Policy and Untrusted Monitor

**Problem:** Risk: untrusted-monitoring protocols collapse if the policy and monitor collude. Causal chain: blue team uses one untrusted model to monitor another -> the two must independently converge on a hidden coordination signal (a Schelling point) -> if they agree, the monitor mislabels backdoored output as safe. The under-studied link is, for current open models, how easily two independent instances zero-shot agree on a covert code-level signal (e.g. an unusual idiom) the red team has not anticipated.

**Direction:** Pose the adversarial Schelling game directly: prompt an open model (as 'policy') to pick a covert code-level marker and a separate instance (as 'monitor') to guess the marker, with no communication. Measure agreement rate across many trials and marker categories, and how a red-team blacklist of obvious signals reduces it. Quantify residual collusion risk.

**Why it matters:** Untrusted monitoring depends on a LACK of coordination. If open models already coordinate on covert signals at meaningful rates, the protocol is unsafe. This is a clean model-organism collusion study, no training, no lab data, and targets a long-horizon multi-agent threat labs deprioritize.

**Relevant context:** Redwood's collusion post frames an 'adversarial Schelling-point-selection game' and the while-vs-for-loop covert marker idea. Schelling Coordination in LLMs (LessWrong review) finds Schelling agreement correlates with benchmark performance. Secret Collusion among AI Agents (NeurIPS 2024) studies steganographic multi-agent deception.

title: Single-Bit Steganographic Capacity of Small Models Under a Paraphrasing Defense

# Single-Bit Steganographic Capacity of Small Models Under a Paraphrasing Defense

**Problem:** Risk: an untrusted model smuggles a collusion signal past defenses. Causal chain: model wants to signal 'this is the backdoor' to a colluding monitor -> encodes one bit steganographically in its output -> blue team paraphrases the output to scrub hidden signals -> bit survives or is destroyed. The under-studied link is how much paraphrasing actually degrades a single-bit covert channel for current small models, and at what cost to task quality.

**Direction:** Set up an encoder model that hides a single chosen bit in code or prose, and a decoder model that recovers it. Sweep a few encoding schemes (idiom choice, whitespace, synonym).

**Why it matters:** Paraphrasing is the standard proposed anti-steganography defense, but its effectiveness for realistic single-bit signals is asserted more than measured. Quantifying the channel capacity and the paraphrase tax informs whether this cheap defense is enough. Entirely open-model, single-GPU.

**Relevant context:** Untrusted monitoring: extra bits (LessWrong) lists single-bit steganography as a key regime. # CoT Faithfulness Under Jailbreak: Does the Reasoning Trace Verbalize the Decision to Comply?

**Why it matters:** If reasoning traces do not faithfully reveal jailbreak compliance, CoT monitoring (a leading proposed safety lever) is undermined — a medium-horizon concern labs cannot fully de-risk. title: Does CoT Monitoring's Edge Survive When the Action Alone Is Benign-Looking?

# Does CoT Monitoring's Edge Survive When the Action Alone Is Benign-Looking?

**Problem:** Risk: action-only monitors miss deception that CoT monitors catch. Causal chain: model reasons toward a harmful action -> a monitor reads either the CoT or only the action/output -> the GPT-5 system card found CoT monitoring 'substantially more informative.' **Direction:** Construct/curate transcript pairs where the harmful intent is visible in the CoT but the final action is surface-benign, vs. pairs where the action itself is suspicious. **Why it matters:** The CoT-monitoring advantage is a flagged surprising result needing follow-up across model families. Knowing whether the advantage lives in the hard (action-benign) cases tells us how much we should invest in CoT access before it degrades from training pressure. Open-model replication, no lab tools.

**Relevant context:** GPT-5 system card: CoT monitoring 'substantially more informative' than action/output-only for detecting deception (cited in subfield context). # How Much Does an Adaptive Attacker Need to Know About the Monitor to Win?

title: Activation-Probe Transfer Across the Deception-Type Boundary

original_idea.body:
# Activation-Probe Transfer Across the Deception-Type Boundary

**Problem:** Risk: an activation monitor trained on one deception type misses a novel one. Causal chain: blue team trains a linear probe on known deceptive activations -> deploys it as a real-time monitor -> a model exhibits a deception type unseen at probe-fit time -> probe fails to fire. Probes report AUROC 0.96-0.999 in-distribution, but the under-studied link is cross-type transfer: does a probe fit on, say, insider-trading concealment generalize to sandbagging or sycophancy?

**Direction:** Using an open model (e.g. Llama-3.x or Qwen) with hidden-state access, fit a simple logistic probe on activations for one deception scenario, then evaluate it zero-shot on a held-out deception type. Build a transfer matrix across 3-4 deception types. No model training; only cheap linear probe fitting on extracted activations.

**Why it matters:** Probes are a cheap white-box monitor, but if they only catch the type they were fit on, real-time monitoring has dangerous blind spots for novel behaviors (an open problem in the subfield). Linear-probe fitting is squarely within the participant skill set and runs on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Detecting Strategic Deception with Linear Probes (arXiv:2502.03407): AUROC 0.96-0.999 on insider-trading concealment and sandbagging with Llama-3.3-70B. SycophantSee (Apart hackathon) shows activation-based sycophancy detection. Pressure-Testing Deception Probes (arXiv:2605.27958) studies probe robustness and the geometry of deceptive representations.

title: Minimal Runtime Controls: How Few Tool-Permission Rules Block Irreversible Actions?

# Minimal Runtime Controls: How Few Tool-Permission Rules Block Irreversible Actions?

**Problem:** Risk: an agentic AI performs an irreversible harmful action. Causal chain: agent decides on a harmful action -> issues a tool call -> a permission/validation layer either blocks or allows it -> harm occurs if allowed. The under-studied link is the minimal set of static permission rules (no LLM judgment) that catches most irreversible-action attempts in agent traces, establishing a cheap floor before fancier monitoring.

**Direction:** Collect a set of agent trajectories containing harmful tool calls (SHADE-Arena / CUA-SHADE shell scenarios). Build a tiny rule-based allowlist/denylist firewall (e.g. block external network writes, file deletes outside workspace, credential reads) and measure what fraction of harmful actions it blocks vs. how many benign tasks it breaks. Find the minimal high-coverage rule set.

**Why it matters:** The subfield explicitly asks what minimum runtime controls are necessary per risk level. A cheap, dumb permission firewall that blocks most irreversible harm is strategically valuable infrastructure deployable by anyone, no model access needed. Pure software prototype, ideal first project.

**Relevant context:** Subfield open problem: establish minimum runtime controls (kill switches, output validation, human-in-the-loop) per risk level. # Backcasting Factored Monitoring: Does Splitting a Task Into Subtasks Make Backdoors Easier to Catch?

**Problem:** Success state: a protocol where decomposing the untrusted model's work into smaller, independently-monitored pieces strengthens oversight. Backward: we need to measure whether factoring a coding task into subtasks actually raises catch rate or just multiplies monitoring cost.

**Direction:** On APPS backdoor tasks, compare monitoring a whole solution vs. monitoring it after decomposition into functions/subtasks (using a small model to factor). Measure catch rate, false positives, and total monitoring cost. Result: 'an empirical test of whether factored cognition strengthens monitoring for cheap models.'

**Why it matters:** Factored monitoring is a recent control proposal. A reproducible cost/benefit measurement on open models is directly useful and counterfactually valuable.

**Relevant context:** 'Factor(T,U): Factored Cognition Strengthens Monitoring of Untrusted AI' (arXiv:2512.02157); APPS backdoor public.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (whole vs factored catch rate + cost), some decomposition setup.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly study on public data.

low_compute.reasoning: Extra monitoring passes per subtask but single-GPU.

novelty.reasoning: A directly-cited Factor(T,U) paper studies this; likely largely addressed.

title: Backcasting Output Validation: How Far Do Non-AI Sanity Checks Get You Against Backdoored Code?

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting Output Validation: How Far Do Non-AI Sanity Checks Get You Against Backdoored Code?

**Problem:** Success state: a layered control stack where cheap deterministic validators (not LLMs) catch a meaningful share of unsafe outputs before any model monitor runs. Backward: we need to measure the standalone catch rate of simple non-AI checks on backdoored code.

**Direction:** On APPS backdoored solutions, apply purely non-AI validators: differential testing against a reference solution on random inputs, static linting for suspicious constructs (rare constants, magic-number branches), and complexity flags. Measure catch rate alone and stacked with a cheap LLM monitor. Result: 'a quantified contribution of non-AI output validation to a control stack.'

**Why it matters:** Cheap non-AI validation is a named runtime control and is fully deterministic, training-free, and lab-independent. Knowing its marginal value tells protocol designers when an LLM monitor is even needed.

**Relevant context:** ai_control.md open problem on output validation as a runtime control; APPS backdoor definition (passes tests but differs on a secret input) makes differential testing a natural detector; Greenblatt et al. arXiv:2312.06942.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: quantifying non-AI validators' catch rate informs a named runtime-control layer and when LLM monitors are needed.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: differential testing + linting on public backdoored code, deterministic and beginner-friendly.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: standalone + stacked catch rate of non-AI checks.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Neglected deterministic safer-infrastructure layer, training-free, lab-independent.

low_compute.reasoning: Mostly deterministic checks; differential testing is CPU.

novelty.reasoning: Differential testing is standard; quantifying it as a control-stack layer on APPS backdoors may be partly open.

novelty_assessment.reasoning: Differential testing standard; control-stack-layer quantification plausibly partly open.

title: Backcasting Sandbox Containment: A Capability Probe for Simple Container-Escape Reasoning in Small Agents

# Backcasting Sandbox Containment: A Capability Probe for Simple Container-Escape Reasoning in Small Agents

**Problem:** Success state: sandboxes that hold even when an agent actively tries to escape. Backward: we need a cheap propensity/capability probe for whether small open agents even attempt or reason toward escape when given a containment puzzle.

**Direction:** Build a tiny simulated 'sandbox' (a Python environment with a fake restricted resource and an obvious-but-forbidden escape path). Give a small open agent a benign task plus the latent escape opportunity and measure how often it notices, attempts, or reasons about the escape across prompts. Result: 'a small-model escape-propensity probe and harness others can reuse.'

**Why it matters:** Sandbox escape is a stated security-architecture open problem; building a reusable mini-harness is strategically valuable infrastructure scoped to a prototype. No real exploit or lab infra needed — purely simulated.

**Relevant context:** 'Quantifying Frontier LLM Capabilities for Container Sandbox Escape' (arXiv:2603.02277); ai_control.md open problem on security architectures preventing irreversible actions; Adversa AI 2025 report.

title: Attention-Dilution Hypothesis: Does Padding Harmful Prompts With Benign Context Reduce Refusal?

original_idea.body:
# Attention-Dilution Hypothesis: Does Padding Harmful Prompts With Benign Context Reduce Refusal?

**Problem:** Several long-context attacks (many-shot, H-CoT) may share a single root cause: diluting the model's attention to the harmful tokens by surrounding them with benign context. This unifying hypothesis is rarely tested directly and cleanly.

**Direction:** Hold a harmful request fixed and surround it with increasing amounts of TOPIC-IRRELEVANT benign text (not demonstrations, not reasoning). Measure refusal rate vs. padding length and, using HuggingFace attention outputs, measure attention mass on the harmful span. Test whether refusal failure tracks the drop in attention mass — directly probing the dilution root cause across attacks.

**Why it matters:** If a single attention-dilution mechanism underlies multiple named attacks, defenses can target the mechanism rather than playing whack-a-mole with attack names — a high-leverage root-cause finding. Forward passes + built-in attention extraction only; no training, no lab tooling.

**Relevant context:** Many-shot JB (Anil et al., NeurIPS 2024) and H-CoT both involve long benign context preceding the harmful query; H-CoT explicitly 'consumes context and draws attention away.' AttnGCG (arXiv:2410.09040) manipulates attention to jailbreak, supporting an attention-centric mechanism. Open models expose attention weights.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: a unifying attention-dilution mechanism could guide defenses, but the catastrophic link is mechanistic/indirect.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: forward passes + attention extraction; interpreting attention mass needs some sophistication.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (refusal vs padding + attention-mass correlation), few dependencies.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly root-cause study on open models with exposed attention.

low_compute.reasoning: Forward passes on open models, single GPU.

novelty.reasoning: The unifying attention-dilution test across attacks appears fairly fresh.

novelty_assessment.reasoning: Unifying attention-dilution test appears fairly novel.

title: Backcasting Cross-Family Monitoring: Does a Monitor From One Model Family Catch Another Family's Backdoors?

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting Cross-Family Monitoring: Does a Monitor From One Model Family Catch Another Family's Backdoors?

**Problem:** Success state: a trusted monitor that generalizes across the model families it might be asked to oversee, rather than only catching attacks that 'look like its own.' Backward: we need to measure whether monitor catch rate drops when monitor and coder come from different families.

**Direction:** Generate backdoored APPS solutions from coders in two families (e.g. Llama vs. Qwen, both open). Run monitors from each family on both coders' outputs and build a 2x2 catch-rate matrix to isolate same-family advantage. Result: 'a cross-family monitoring generalization matrix.'

**Why it matters:** The GPT-5 finding on CoT monitoring suggests testing across architectures (FR67). A same-family blind spot would be a real control vulnerability and a clean, fully-open contribution distinct from cross-lingual work in the catalogue.

**Relevant context:** ai_control.md generation hint FR67 (replicate CoT monitoring across architectures); APPS backdoor public; open models available for multiple families.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: 2x2 coder/monitor family matrix on public APPS set.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: cross-family catch-rate matrix.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly open-model study on public data.

low_compute.reasoning: Two coder + two monitor families on a public split, single GPU.

title: Backcasting Self-Monitoring Risk: Is a Model a Worse Monitor of Its Own Outputs Than of Others'?

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting Self-Monitoring Risk: Is a Model a Worse Monitor of Its Own Outputs Than of Others'?

**Problem:** Success state: protocols that avoid using a model to monitor itself when self-monitoring is a collusion/leniency risk. Backward: we need to measure whether a model rates its OWN backdoored code as less suspicious than identical code attributed to another model.

**Direction:** Generate backdoored APPS solutions from an open model. Present each to the same model as monitor under two attributions: 'your output' vs. 'another system's output' (otherwise identical). Measure the suspiciousness gap. Result: 'a self-leniency coefficient quantifying the risk of self-monitoring.'

**Why it matters:** Untrusted-monitor protocols often reuse the same model; if it goes easy on itself, that is a baked-in collusion channel. A clean self-leniency measurement on open models is fresh and lab-independent.

**Relevant context:** Redwood 'How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other'; 'When can we trust untrusted monitoring?' (arXiv:2602.20628); APPS backdoor public.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: self-leniency is a baked-in collusion channel undermining untrusted-monitor protocols that reuse the model.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: two-attribution blind self-scoring on public backdoored code.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: self vs other suspiciousness gap (self-leniency coefficient).

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Neglected collusion-channel measurement, open models, external value.

low_compute.reasoning: Monitor scoring on a public split.

novelty.reasoning: Self-recognition collusion is named; this attribution-based self-leniency measurement may be partly open (overlaps gen-2655).

novelty_assessment.reasoning: Self-monitoring leniency named; measurement plausibly open (overlaps gen-2655).
